L361: We wrote custom HIP kernels for the layer-norm operation and for several subroutines used in the Muon optimizer.
L362: #### V-B 1 Muon
L363: The Muon optimizer combines Stochastic Gradient Descent with momentum with an added orthogonalization step on the momentum-updated gradient. The approximate orthogonalization is performed via a few iterations of the Newton–Schulz (NS) method on the full momentum-updated gradient matrix. Note that by construction, Muon can only be applied to 2D parameters; other parameters (such as 1D norms and 3D convolutional layers) are optimized with AdamW.
L364: Our custom kernels optimize the weight and momentum update steps and the NS step.
L365: Our weight and momentum update kernels are fused HIP multi-tensor kernels, similar to the fused AdamW kernels in Apex (cite132†NVIDIA, 2025 ), and are invoked via multi_tensor_apply: (i) a momentum kernel that updates the FP32 momentum buffer and emits BF16 inputs for the NS method, and (ii) an update kernel that applies decoupled weight decay and the update to FP32 master weights. Both kernels process lists of parameter shards in chunks with instruction-level parallelism (ILP) and coalesce memory accesses.
L366: Denote a 2D tensor of trainable parameters as $w$, the associated gradient at step $t$ as $g_{t}$, and the momentum buffer as $m_{t}$. The momentum kernel computes the input tensor for the NS procedure:
L367: 
L368:  | $\displaystyle m_{t}$  | $\displaystyle=\mu\,m_{t-1}+g_{t},$  | $\displaystyle\mathrm{NS_{in}}$  | $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}m_{t}&\text{(no Nesterov)}\\
L369: g_{t}+\mu\,m_{t}&\text{(Nesterov)}\end{cases}$  |
L370: where $\mu$ is a fixed scalar. The output of the NS procedure is the weight update that is used by the second kernel to compute:
L371: 
L372:  | $\displaystyle w$  | $\displaystyle\leftarrow(1-\eta\,\delta)\,w,$  | $\displaystyle w$  | $\displaystyle\leftarrow w-\lambda\,\mathrm{NS_{out}}.$  |

L374: Here, $\eta$ is the base learning rate that is shared with AdamW-optimized parameters, $\delta$ is the weight decay factor and $\lambda$ is the adjusted learning rate for Muon.
L375: All arithmetic accumulates are in FP32; BF16 is used to reduce bandwidth for gradients/NS inputs and optional shadow weights. Separating momentum and Nesterov-update from the weight update (i) produces bandwidth-friendly BF16 NS inputs, (ii) keeps master-weight traffic isolated, and (iii) allows distinct launch/stream tuning for NS vs. update.
L376: In practice, these two memory-linear passes substantially cut optimizer overhead, such that iteration time is dominated by model compute and communication rather than optimizer step time.

L95: LLM-based PyTorch/kernel optimization can be viewed as a search for an optimal solution, and an explore-exploit tradeoff emerges from this search process. Exploration builds a broad base of valid solutions to avoid premature convergence, whereas exploitation concentrates effort on the best existing solutions.
L96: We analyze how system components interact in multi-agent PyTorch optimization systems, focusing on the explore–exploit tradeoff, and identify an optimal configuration for PyTorch inference optimization.

However, the main takeaway is that, compared to the default PIKE-O variant, which combines exploitative and exploratory strategies, the more exploitative configurations yield better performance for this type of task. Notably, while PIKE-O (`mut,npar,1isl,EO,SL`) consistently remains the top performer, the second and third places have switched, with PIKE-O (`mut,npar,1isl,EO`) outpacing PIKE-O (`mut,npar,1isl`).

By reducing the number of islands, limiting parallelism, and minimizing the elite archive, we achieve a focused, mutation-driven optimization that closely aligns with the strengths observed in PIKE-B.

L104@P1: Transformers and Their Computational Challenges:
L105@P1: Deep learning algorithms, notably convolutional neural
L106@P1: networks (CNNs), have significantly advanced fields such as
L107@P1: computer vision [32], speech recognition [30], and natural
L108@P1: language processing [2]. More recently, transformer-based
L109@P1: architectures have emerged as the dominant paradigm,
L110@P1: surpassing traditional recurrent and convolutional models
L111@P1: across numerous AI domains [2], [23], [29]. The core innovation of transformers lies in the self-attention mechanism,
L112@P1: which enables the model to capture global dependencies
L113@P1: across input sequences by computing pairwise token interactions [29]. This results in superior performance in tasks
L114@P1: requiring long-range context understanding.

L199@P2: III. NX-CGRA
L200@P2: NX-CGRA (see Figure 1 (a)) is a programmable hardware accelerator designed to support heterogeneous transformer inference workloads at the edge. Its microarchitecture is organized as a CGRA tailored for the efficient
L201@P2: execution of both linear and non-linear computation kernels
L202@P2: through a multiple instruction, multiple data (MIMD)-style
L203@P2: execution model.
L204@P2: A. Array Topology and Execution Model
L205@P2: The core of NX-CGRA consists of a two-dimensional
L206@P2: heterogeneous array of PEs and Memory-Operation Blocks
L207@P2: (MOBs) interconnected via a switchless mesh torus interconnect network (see Figure 1 (b)). Each core executes a
L208@P2: microcode of the target application, statically scheduled
L209@P2: during compile time. This design choice enables flexible
L210@P2: and fine-grained scheduling of operations, particularly valuable for irregular workloads and non-uniform computation
L211@P2: graphs typical of transformer models.
L212@P2: To facilitate MIMD execution, the array supports distributed instruction decoding and local register files. Each
L213@P2: core is equipped with its own lightweight instruction buffer
L214@P2: and controller to execute its assigned micro-operations.
